query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing approximately 1–2 atomic percent tungsten (W) during processing of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will enhance its strength–ductility balance and improve its stability under long-term mechanical loading, temperature fluctuations, and corrosive conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure exhibiting good but suboptimal strength and plasticity.
generation.intervention: Microalloying by adding ~1–2 at% tungsten during alloy processing.
generation.conditions: Performance tested under industrially relevant scenarios including extreme and fluctuating temperatures, sustained mechanical (creep) loads, and corrosive environments. The tungsten must remain in solid solution without forming unwanted secondary phases.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced short-range order (SRO) and modified grain boundary chemistry. Tungsten atoms, due to their refractory nature and solid solution behavior, are expected to stabilize the lamellar microstructure and impede grain boundary sliding.
generation.mechanism: Tungsten microalloying is anticipated to increase local chemical ordering, which raises the energy barrier for dislocation motion and improves grain boundary pinning. The increased SRO hinders vacancy-mediated dislocation climb and grain boundary migration, thereby simultaneously raising strength and ductility while also improving creep resistance. Moreover, tungsten’s high melting point contributes to improved microstructural and corrosion stability under extreme temperature fluctuations.
generation.predicted_outcome: The tungsten-doped alloy will show a higher yield strength, improved ductility, a reduced creep rate, and enhanced corrosion resistance compared to the baseline alloy.
generation.baseline: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy without tungsten addition.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected when tungsten remains uniformly distributed at low additions (1–2 at%). If tungsten segregation or secondary phase formation occurs (e.g., at higher than targeted concentrations or under inappropriate processing conditions), the improvements may not be realized.
generation.uncertainty: While the proposed mechanism is supported by known effects of SRO and grain boundary stabilization as well as tungsten’s refractory behavior, the exact quantitative improvements and potential for unexpected phase behavior under long-term service conditions require further verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples under identical processing conditions: one set of the baseline AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy and one set microalloyed with 1–2 at% tungsten. Subject both sets to mechanical testing (e.g., tensile tests and long-term creep tests) under cyclic and elevated temperature conditions, as well as to corrosion testing in environments representative of service conditions. Use advanced microscopy to assess the microstructural features (lamellar structure, grain boundaries, tungsten distribution) before and after testing.
measurements: Yield strength and ultimate tensile strength
Long-term creep rate under constant load at elevated temperatures
Microstructural analysis via TEM/SEM to detect changes in lamellar morphology and tungsten distribution
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tungsten microalloyed samples do not show statistically significant improvements in mechanical properties (yield strength, ductility, and creep resistance) and corrosion performance compared to the baseline, or if tungsten addition results in deleterious microstructural changes (e.g., formation of harmful secondary phases or tungsten segregation), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The SRO in the grain interior hinders grain boundary migration because, when a grain boundary sweeps its grain matrix, the chemical SRO in the swept volume will be destroyed as the boundary migration alters the crystallographic orientation of the swept matrix (). The grain size–dependent chemical ordering in grain boundary and matrix stabilizes boundary network and mitigates softening effects, deserving careful attention and further study. Note that the imposed straining rate (108 s−1) in the simulations, which can adequately enable true dislocation dynamics (), is still several orders of magnitude higher than that of conventional laboratory experiments. When sufficiently lowering the strain rate, thermally activated diffusional processes, including vacancy-mediated dislocation climb and Coble creep, can take place and decrease the strength. Because chemical SRO considerably reduces and localizes diffusion (), it is tempting to hypothesize that the strength difference between RSS and SRO systems will widen even further at reduced strain rates and/or elevated temperatures.
